utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, while we are all waiting, this is a witness the Prosecution has presented as 92 ter. And I will show to the witness two documents, perhaps one photo, and I will lead him in chief, perhaps, for 15 minutes, 20 minutes, so it should not take that long, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps also to save time, the first document I would like to show to the witness will be ter number 02888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name on the record, please.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Buco Kemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Buco, did you give a witness statement on the 23rd of February, 1996, to the ICTY investigators? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness statement, the English version, could be put onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Buco, can you look at the statement and tell Their Honours whether that is the statement which you gave to the ICTY investigators, and whether that's indeed your signature, as it appears to be?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the witness's first name Buco or is it Kemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is your first name Kemal? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: My first name is Kemal; my last name is Buco.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You're welcome. Mr. President, if we can see the whole document, please, the next page and the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Buco, did you also have a chance to review this statement in my office a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And after having read this statement, did you clarify a few issues in this statement? And you also provided some additional information about the death of a girl and a few remarks about the general situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mrs. Court Usher, if we could have 65 ter number 02893, please, displayed. And while that's being done -- I don't think we have received it yet. I will repeat the number. It is 0283. This should be an information report dated the 29th of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to avoid confusion, this first number, 2930, is incorrect. The correct one is 0283.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm very obliged to you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Thank you very much, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic, for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm told it's 2893. That's the number I had initially read out. 02893.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed. I just want to make sure, Mr. Tapuskovic, you have the number now, 2893.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have it now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Buco, can you have a look perhaps at the B/C/S version on the right side of your screen. That's your language. Are these the clarifications you gave in my office a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in regard to these two documents, the witness statement of February 1996 and this information report of a few days ago, are you satisfied -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to get my mic off but it isn't responding. I thought there might have been a connection there. It's off now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we might have resolved it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In relation to these two documents, Mr. Buco, are you satisfied, and can you attest now to the Court, that the witness statement and the information report accurately reflect your evidence and the answers you would give now, if asked, about the same matters under oath?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buco. Mr. President, if we could have two exhibit numbers for these documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number P158. Sorry, P158 is for the statement bearing 65 ter number 2888, and P159 will be the document bearing 65 ter number 2893.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Court Usher. Mr. President, with your leave, a few questions from Mr. Buco to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one is: What is your profession, Mr. Buco?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I am an engineer of agronomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what do you currently do for a living?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I'll retired now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And back in 1994 in Sarajevo, what was your profession then?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Before I retired, I had been working in the republican ministry as a state security inspector. During the war I was asked to assist them in collecting statements from persons who were victims of war in order to prepare the documents for the Hague Tribunal in issuing indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And doing that, did you have to wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you, as part of your duties, attend crime scenes?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No. I only took statements from the victims, and based on these statements I compiled my own reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness could be shown 65 ter number 02887, which is a document dated 24th November 1994 and entitled "Official Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My question to the witness would be, while this is being retrieved: Is that one of the reports you would draw up as part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you draft this report, Mr. Buco?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Their Honours what this report is about, very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: It was a report about an incident which took place on the 23rd of November, 1994. A team of experts visited the scene together with two ballistic experts and a technician in order to assess how this situation occurred, where the bullet had come from, what kind of bullet it was. Based on their statements and reports, I prepared my own report; and also on the basis of statements taken later from the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would just like you to comment on one or two sentences from this report, and on the English version, on the left side, it starts a little bit after the middle of the page, "At 1530 hours..." and the same should be in the B/C/S investigation.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I would like to quote four lines down from that paragraph, and I'll read it out slowly. "The bullet was fired from south or south-east (in relation to the area of the tram which was hit from the direction of Grbavica) penetrated into the tram through the open window (the last window next to the connecting platform of the tram on the left). On the top right corner of the last window on the right in the front section of the tram, two traces were seen caused by the bullet which hit the tram." Do you see that, Mr. Buco?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have two questions. The first one - and you might have touched upon that in your previous answer - based on what did you put into the report the direction of fire coming from Grbavica? Did somebody tell you? Did you find it out yourself?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: This was based on the ballistic reports, and on the basis of the reports of these ballistics experts, I put this in my report, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you listed the names of these two ballistics experts on --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the second question I wanted to ask you: Here it says - and these are your words - that the bullet penetrated into the tram through the open window. At the same time, you say that two traces were seen caused by the bullet which hit the tram. Can you explain what you meant when you wrote this sentence down?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: As I said, based on the ballistic reports, this is what I wrote, literally as they this described it, and that's how I put it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buco. Let me show you one photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is P -- it's already an existing exhibit, P88. Can the participants in the courtroom see the picture?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, we don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, I should be a bit more patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While I do that, Mr. Buco, and here we do have the picture, can you point to this photograph and tell, if you can - and I believe you need the assistance of the usher - if you can point to Their Honours the location where you believe the incident that you investigated took place.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: The ballistic expert established that this location was between the secondary school of engineering and the Marshal Tito barracks. On this side here there is also the museum there and the museum of the revolution. Are these the two locations that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So these two crosses you made, that's in between where you say the incident took place about the trams?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: That's what I had been told. Let us make this very clear. This was what the ballistics claimed, and also the witnesses who gave statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this exhibit could be tendered, could you given a number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And lastly, if the witness could be -- could be shown another exhibit - and this will be the last one - which is 65 ter number 00059, a document dated 15 December 1994 and entitled "Official Note."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Buco, can you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Their Honours what it is?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: It's a note that I made based on witness statements who sustained injuries and who were in the hospital. It wasn't done on the same day. It took a few days for them to recover a little, for the patients to be able to give statements, and we asked them to describe what and how it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And does this report relate to the same incident we have been discussing with the previous report you drafted?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could also have an exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be become Exhibit number P161.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this, Madam Court Deputy. One or two more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Buco, did you ever hear as part of your professional activities that shots wounding Bosnian Muslim citizens, indeed citizens of Sarajevo within the territory controlled by the Bosnian Muslim army, were shot by Bosnian Muslims? Have you any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I think that was absurd. But, no, I never heard of any such incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the problem? I didn't have that translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher give the lectern to my colleague, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before Defence counsel takes the floor, I have a small question to put to you. If I have understood you correctly, you were a state security inspector of the republic and you were working for the state ministry. What is your exact title? I think that is your exact title. And you drafted your report on the basis of a report provided by two ballistics experts and two technicians. I would like to know who these ballistics experts worked for, which state ministry. These technicians also, who these people were, who reported to whom? And which ministry did they work for, these two experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is written in the note their titles and who they worked for. As for me, before the war, I worked at the Ministry of the Interior, State Ministry of the Interior, as a state security inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked a question by the Judge and you must answer it. You don't answer it by saying, "It is written in the note." Now let us know for whom do they work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They worked for the Ministry of the Interior, the cantonal ministry, which is now the canton of Sarajevo. And they were this ministry's officials. At the time it was called the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you belonged to the same ministry as the two inspectors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was just seconded to them, to assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course the Prosecution has decided which tactic to apply in this case, and they questioned this witness for about half an hour. I don't know how much time I will need. I am not going into this tactic that is currently being applied by the Prosecution and put to me in such a situation. What I'm interested in is to know how much time has been allotted to me for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that immediately after the break, and to try to survive as a Defence counsel the next 20 minutes in order to put together all these things introduced by the Prosecution, all these contradictory issues and things. I am not a magician and I cannot do that under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will be reasonable in its allocation of time to you for cross-examination. Start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. Witness, I would try to ask you the following, and after that I'm going to seek some explanations from you: Is it really true that these two statements that you made - one long an ago and the other one that was given to us the day before yesterday - that they actually reflect the situation as it was; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: They are based on all of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also fair to say that you stand by that is the truth, what you said years ago and what you also said in this supplemental information given to me the day before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me now, you are an engineer of agronomy; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As an engineer of agronomy, you took statements from witnesses relating to very delicate issues and situations involving the killings caused by snipers and other plights of the people; is that true?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So my direct question is, how did you have enough courage with your expertise of an engineer of agronomy - I know what it involves; I sometimes plant a tree myself - how do you think you were able to give any kind of assessment about these issues?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I had been working in the police for ten years before the war. To be precise, state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the murders and the killings of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. So, all of your conclusion were based, firstly, on taking statements from the witnesses themselves and, secondly, things that other people told you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you check anything yourself once you had these documents in front of you in terms of whether these documents faithfully reflected the situation on the ground? I mean as reflected in your witness examinations.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: That was not part of my job description.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps have -- were you a boss or something?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I was the so-called criminal inspector, but I never really was one. That was just my assignment. Just to make this clear, I was just a helper. As I said at the outset, I was helping the team collect statements from victims in order to have enough material and documents for The Hague, based on the statements of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in order to produce enough material for this Tribunal, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, was it not your duty to do your best to collect the sort of evidence that might be helpful to the court? Was it not your duty to check certain things before ...

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, anybody was free to tell you whatever they liked and you would have taken it at face value; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, I don't understand. Can you tell Chamber, please, how exactly did you go about this?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I based everything on the statements provided by the victims, people who came to grief in one way or another. And probably all those victims will be testifying in this trial, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did those people know, the victims? They had been injured. What were they able to tell you? They had nearly lost their lives. What were they able to tell you, or was it you who told them what had occurred?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, I never let anyone say anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pretty soon the interpreter is going to be asking you to observe a pause between question and answer. Do you understand, Witness? For the benefit of the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my mistake. I always get carried away. It's always at the expense of the accused, but what can I do? Sometimes I'm just not fully in control. I just don't have full control over the pace of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, do you abide by these documents that were placed before the Chamber by the OTP? You confirm that they are absolutely true and faithful, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I abide by whatever I heard from any of the witnesses and by whatever I wrote based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this has not been interpreted, but I must ask you again. Did the witnesses tell you where they had been hit from? Did they tell you all these things in the condition in which they were in when they were brought to a hospital? Did you bring them there? Did anybody else bring them there? Do you know what their condition was? Was it not the fact that they were unable, because of their condition, to determine all these things? But then police inspectors came along and they made suggestions to them as to where they had been hit from.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Nobody made any suggestions to anyone else. Nobody made any representations to anyone else. There were ballistics experts and they determined where the bullets had come from. As for witnesses who were injured, they told us what they had been through. That's all they ever told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it is your evidence that none of the witnesses ever told you where they had been hit from, where the bullet had come from, and they weren't able to in the condition that they were in.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, nobody ever told me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You still consider yourself to be a top-notch expert, although you were never trained in the science of ballistics. You know nothing about snipers; you know nothing about the various calibres of these weapons, do you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I never said I was an expert. Again, I repeat: I'm no expert. All I did was what I was told to do: Take statements, write up reports, statements/report. They're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Based on such reports, a person here stands indicted of killing God knows how many people, based on such reports?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Are you expecting me to tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me if it was based on such reports that it was ascertained that someone had been killed by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. While producing these reports, why did you never ask an officer to help you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: You go and call an officer to help you. You have many officers around here, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand the answer. The question was: "While producing these reports, why did you never ask an officer to help you?" Don't get excited. Just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need. May I be allowed to continue? There was no need for me to do that. I had a team doing just that. People who were experts in the field, ballistics experts, they ascertained where the shots had come from and what the bullets were. Am I supposed to go on philosophising, asking further explanations, when there's no need for that at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, what I said was I didn't understand the answer, not I didn't understand the question. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't even know what my language is called, but in the Bosnian language, what the witness told me was that I should myself call officers to do that. He said, "You should be the one calling the officers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The comment I made had nothing to do with that, Mr. Tapuskovic. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour, but I'm sure you're doing your best to keep this cross-examination normal. I don't think this is the right thing for a witness to do, to answer me back like this. I can ask him a direct question. I'll tell you, I'll be calling generals to be testifying about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not call in a simple military officer at the time, a captain or someone like that, someone who knew about weapons, to look into this for you, so that you might be able to present better evidence before this court? We would have had an expert assessing evidence and that would have spelled less trouble for us. Can you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: There was never an order for me to do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the witness said that they were part of a team, that there were ballistics experts who did that. He didn't say he was on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I allowed it because this question is a little different. It's asking him more specifically, why didn't he call in a military officer, a captain or someone like that. That's why I allowed it. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was never an order for me to do anything like that regarding the army, the military. We never used any assistance from the military in that sense. We believed that our ballistic experts were perfectly capable of resolving the situation and ascertaining where the bullets were coming from. That was, after all, their job, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic, you have the answer. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I understand you correctly, you're trying to say that your own police superiors ordered you to never, under any conditions, call in any military officers who knew about weapons. You were to get the job done just like that; no supervision, no experts involved. And then you just submit the whole thing to the Hague Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Waespi is standing to say that the witness did not say that precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, and also there were experts, so you cannot put to him that he said -- you know, he was told not to bring experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you should move on. I think this particular line of questioning has been exhausted. Let's move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will move on, but I still think I have not received a good answer. Can the witness explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- it's for the Chamber now to make up its mind as to the credibility of the witness on this issue, and I have instructed you to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to raise something that I was going to raise at the very end, if there's time left. Perhaps I can manage this before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness if he knew anything about his own units. He was, after all, a police inspector, wasn't he? So what I want to know is how familiar the witness is with the numbers of police officers in the middle of Sarajevo, in the middle of the war, going about their work, all of them armed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know that there were about 20.000 armed police officers walking around Sarajevo. Were you armed yourself?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We had a witness here, a well-regarded witness, someone from NATO, who took an oath here and testified that there was not a single child in Sarajevo at the time that was unarmed, yet you, as a police inspector, claim never to have carried a weapon. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I never carried a weapon; it's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your police administration based, and how many armed people were there? You say you weren't armed, but were there police officers who were armed - machine-guns, pistols, howitzers even?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: It's a ridiculous question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The police had no APCs, did they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have a single mortar, did they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, none. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to ask you this question as if I were a prosecutor not a defence counsel. The police were never involved in defensive operations, were they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Sarajevo during that offensive?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo throughout. That's easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yet you say that the police never took part, with their own forces numbering about 15.000 or 20.000 people, never took part at least in that one offensive in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: What offensive are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the offensive that was launched on the 15th and the 16th along all the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either, do you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, then, you probably know nothing about the positions of the BH army, do you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me ask you this: You were born in Sarajevo; right.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At least you're familiar with Sarajevo's geography; right? Sarajevo was a well-liked town. We all liked it. We all went there. We all got along fine.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you at least know the streets?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know the streets?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know the hills?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know the hills?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Not their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know where Trebevic is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: That's where the aggressors were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They were at Debelo Brdo, too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, the aggressors were all around Sarajevo on all the hills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic and the witness, if you look at the transcript, you will see that the interpreters are asking you to slow down. You're overlapping, so you must both exercise discipline and rigour in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, the aggressor was at Debelo Brdo, too?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The aggressor was at Mojmilo, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the foot of the hill or at the top of the hill?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: The aggressor took all of the elevations, all the high points around Sarajevo, and we were down there. We were cannon fodder. We were just clay pigeons for them to fire at. And they fired at will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what the indictment says. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, no. We were clay pigeons, I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Mojmilo ridge? It's 3 kilometres long. And you know the lay of the land. You know that the hill was under the command of the army of Republika Srpska, under their control; right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything. All I know is that my flat was shelled from that side once; then twice. I moved to another flat again. The shells came from the same side. The third time around I was shelled in my own office at Skenderija. It all came from the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: You'd do well to believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you, that this was the case. But let me ask you about your office.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: At Skenderija, that's where the office was. It was across the way from the centre. What's it called?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I hadn't finished my question.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about your office. Your office was part of this police station. You never carried any weapons, thank God for that. But there were a lot of armed police officers there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, not in my building, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A total of how many people there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know how many people worked in your office?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, not in my office. I'm talking about the whole building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were an inspector. I know that you had your own office to yourself and that you were the only person in that office, and you were preparing all these documents that we are now considering.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, not just this. I did a whole lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the total number of police officers in that building.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not even an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know how many police stations there were in Sarajevo with armed police officers?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The police officers were not in the least interested in defending the citizens of Sarajevo who were being shelled from those hills all around?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: The police had its own job cut out for it. It was the usual police job, the sort of job that police officers always do. We all know what the role of the police is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the role of the police is what I know it to be, which is, above all, to see to it that none of the citizens are killed, would that seem to imply that you know nothing about the Serb, Muslim and Croat civilians being killed down there, you know, by people in Sarajevo who were under the control of the BH army? You know nothing about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are going to take a break for 20 minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must have dropped at least half the questions that I had for this witness. However, 15 minutes is not even enough for five questions. I can start and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness is here to testify about countless incidents. I understand he is no expert, and that's why I have dropped at least two-thirds of my questions. Only experts can answer these questions. However, I am compelled to ask him a number of questions. I have very few documents here. I'm giving up everything that he seems to know nothing about, that is, the hills around Sarajevo although he is a native of Sarajevo. I do have to ask the witness about these two documents that were tendered by the OTP. D158; that is the statement dated the 23rd of February; and the other statement, the 65 ter statement - I'm not sure what the numbers are - 02893. This is the statement that he provided some days ago. I do have to bring up these two, which will take at least 15 minutes, and then I will be showing you those documents. If we could please have the first statement brought up on our screens, page 1. The number is P158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, if on line -- page 70, line 24 and 25, is mentioned the name and the name should be redacted. Unfortunately, I was careless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just page 1, is that at page 1, Mr. Prosecutor? I won't be mentioning any names at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, I am not mentioning your document. I was mentioning something that I said earlier, unrelated to your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us not waste time. Could we then have P158? It was tendered a minute ago. Page 2. I have several questions based on page 2 of that document. I'll just be mentioning his name. I've nothing on my screen, on either of my screens. There's nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We now have something on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here is the beginning of your statement. I'm not mentioning you, but in the second sentence you say: "From May 1994 to March 1995 I volunteered" --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: In the genocide department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not that far along yet. I'm about to tell you that. You worked in the genocide department between 1994 and March 1995 in Sarajevo and no where else. That's what you claim. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain to the Chamber about 1994 and 1995. What was this genocide about? If you could please provide a detailed explanation. What exactly constituted this genocide? Was that the firing going on between the two parties or was there a genocide? And what exactly do you mean when you say "genocide?"

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: It's stated very clearly. I worked as an inspector. I collected documents about crimes that the security services centre dealt with. It's not only in reference to this period of time. It's not only between 1994 and 1995. It was throughout the war. Whatever was going on, people would come to see me and to give statements. These statements were something that I wrote down. That was part of a final report. And then documents were compiled for the benefit of this Tribunal from the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, just to make that perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that is just not right, is it? It reads: "Between May 1994," not throughout the war, as you say. "Between May 1994 and March 1995, I worked on a voluntary basis as an inspector for Sarajevo in the genocide department." No other position is indicated here, nothing about the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is expressly stated here "genocide Sarajevo" and the period of time indicated here, which is also the period of time covered by the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic. Can you please explain what exactly constituted genocide in Sarajevo in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: You misunderstand me. I did work there between 1994 and 1995, I mean collecting information. But it wasn't information in relation to that period alone. It was information in relation to the entire duration of the war and what happened to people, various genocidal situations. They came to me. I collected all of this. There are volumes and volumes, endless volumes of statements. It's not just a handful of statements. Those were countless people giving statements. I lose track exactly of how many there were who I interviewed, who came to me to give their statement. It's not only about this period here, 1994 to 1995. The whole war was a genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I appreciate your explanation, but please, in your second statement, why didn't you say so and correct it in the way you just did? In the first statement you categorical said that you dealt only with the Sarajevo area in the years of 1994 and 1995, not before or after.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: We still don't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course we don't.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I was based in Sarajevo. Do you understand that? My office was in Sarajevo, but people from various places all over Bosnia-Herzegovina came to see me and give statements. Do you understand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to waste any more time. It will be up to the Chamber to evaluate this. You did tell untruths someplace.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I never said any untruthful things, and I adhere to everything I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see now. I'm going to skip a lot of questions. In paragraph 3, when you talk about tram number 263, you said that: "At around 1530 it was hit by one bullet of undetermined calibre which splintered and wounded Hafiza Karacic and Sabina Sabanic. The bullet went through the rubber part where the tram carriages are joined, so it was not obvious to the driver that the tram had been shot. The bullet was of a fragmentation type." You, as an expert, stated this.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No. I said that I wrote my reports based on the reports and evidence collected by ballistics experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Waespi is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic repeatedly refers to the witness as expert, and he said a number of times before that he is it not an expert, that he did what he did. So please don't misrepresent the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. He has expressly, in answer to you, said that he was not an expert. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As an expert in agronomy, you just said the following, in paragraph 3, towards the end: "The driver in this case mentioned hearing a burst of fire and passengers referring to stones being thrown at the tram, indicating that there was more than one bullet." Does that correspond to the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will skip everything else pertaining to this statement.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: There is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course there is no need for that. You are not an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, stop wasting time and stop the comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let us look at the second statement of yours that you made the other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 02893. If we can have it in front of the witness, please. It has been tendered a short while ago. 02893, that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's Exhibit P159. And it's not a statement; it's an information report written by us but shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was shown to the witness. He confirmed its authenticity. And in both the documents he said he stood by what they contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I don't know what you want me to discuss now with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will continue. In paragraph 2 concerning the statement given on the 23rd of November, 1996, it says that: "The bullet passed through the rubber part where the tram carriages are joined. The witness says that he cannot really explain that sentence. Both reports say that the bullet came through the window. The witness said that he might have made a mistake, or it was mistakenly translated into English." Now can you please explain to the Chamber, not to me, how is it possible for you to say something like this the other day and to confirm both your statements? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is what happened. Concerning the bullet passing through the rubber part, that's not correct because that's not something that I said. I think that an interpreter made a mistake when he was translating from B/C/S into English. These two women were close to this rubber section of the tram, and that was where the mistake was made, the two women who were shot. And the bullet, as far as the information I received from the ballistics expert, the bullet passed through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's such a huge discrepancy I'm not going to deal with that any longer?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: It's not such a huge discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I always tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be up to Their Honours to decide that. Now, the next passage, the witness says that on the 23rd of November, 1994, he stayed in the area. "The trams were hit only very briefly because it was very dangerous." I see from this that you were on the spot and yet you said that you never visited the scene.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I never visited the scene when it happened. Of course I didn't go to the scene and I wasn't even then there. We just passed by the location in a car. We went to Remiza to make the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this is also not true. When you made the statement the other day, you didn't tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: I wasn't on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you did?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said that you stayed very briefly on the location.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No. We just briefly passed by the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This will again be evaluated by the Chamber. At the end of your statement, if we can please look at the next page, can you see it? The end of your statement, and this is what you say here. "The witness also said that his main job was not to go to crime scenes and do investigations. His prime task was to collect evidence for the Hague Tribunal based on information he got from witnesses all over Bosnia." This is something that you mentioned today, but in this specific document it is obvious that you did go to crime scenes at least once.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No. I again ascertain that we passed by the place where the incident occurred. Even if we had wanted to remain there, we couldn't have done so because snipers were still active. I'm not a fool to risk my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. He stated clearly that the witness also said "that his main job was not to go to crime scenes," and, Mr. Tapuskovic, you put to the witness that "You did go to the crime scenes."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I just put it to the witness that he said that he had only visited the crime scene once.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm satisfied with this answer, but I would like to present to the Chamber a document, DD00-02428, and I would like to draw the attention of Their Honours to the B/C/S version. It's dated the 24th of November, which is exactly around the time of this incident. I would like you, Your Honours, to look at the B/C/S version. I'm not going to ask anything of the witness, and I would just like to show you how -- what procedure was applied in these kinds of incidents. Could you please take a look at this document, DD00-02428, dated the 24th of November, 1994. Your Honours, please just look at those pages, 1; then page 2. Please look at this. Now page 3. There is another page and there's another page as well. That's the last one. This is the basis on which you are supposed to establish the truth. These kinds of documents which are blurry, the things that can probably show how the indictment is unfounded, they are so blurred that they are totally illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think I do have an English translation of the document; and second, I don't understand the question he is putting to the witness. Does he blame him for the quality of -- the blurred quality of this image, or -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is impossible to translate this document to any language at all. No one can read this. This is -- this was intentionally blurred because presumably this will show the whole truth about the incidents from that period. And that was done on purpose, probably by the witness that we have here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does the witness have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: This is something that I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to expedite my questioning, if you, Your Honours, would just grant me a few minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, I must warn you against impugning the character of the witness without any foundation. You said that this was something probably done by the witness. Do you have any basis for saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document deals with the events produced by his department, and it could have been greatly helpful in shedding light on the tram incident, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was not my question. It is irresponsible of counsel to make wild accusations. Do you have any kind of evidence that this blurring of the document was done by this witness? I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I apologise to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does he know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's an apology well made, and in the future you must avoid wild accusations, because counsel has certain responsibilities and a code of conduct, certain ethical standards that must be observed. You went over the line. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am prepared to take responsibility for this. I will not comment any further. I have my opinion, and I thought it would have been helpful for you to look at this. Maybe I shouldn't have done so. I take note of your caution, and I will take due care in future when these kinds of things arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask the witness this: Does he know -- and there's a document that I have obtained. It has about 700 or 800 pages, and only the relative pages are to be translated. It's a war log of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this war log of the BH army for the 18th of November - that is the day when this little girl was killed - it says under the date, 18th November 1994, and I quote, and I would like to ask the witness if he is aware of this. Okay, a child was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I am following which incidents counsel means. If he refers to a killing of a young girl by a sniper that's referred to by the witness in his information report - Your Honours, that's paragraph 4 of this note - it says that the incident occurred a few days after the shooting of the trams, which would be after the 23rd of November. But you're asking him something about the 18th of November. Just so that you are aware of this discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What incident are you talking about? And after this, one more question, Mr. Tapuskovic, and then you are to wind up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be this document and then another document produced by UNPROFOR. I have an abundance of other documents as well. Your Honours, I'm quoting, and I would like to ask the witness if he knows that in the war log of the BH army, an entry dated 18 November 1994, it says as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "In the Sarajevo battlefield, our units only opened fire intermittently during the day. However, there was a fierce exchange of fire between UNPROFOR and the aggressor at around 9.00 p.m. from small arms. As a result of the shelling of the city, a child was killed." This is what is written in the war log of the BH army. I'm just asking if he knows about this.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since this incident that we discussed happened on the 23rd of November, I have an UNPROFOR report only partly translated. It's an English version. DD00-0436. So United Nations, UNPROFOR. And later on I will tender this for identification as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to read just a small portion relating to the 23rd of November, 1994. Let me read this. It's page 2, an introduction, and this next page, if we can please have this in front of the Judges, because the gentleman cannot speak English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to read it to you. Yes, that's it. Midway down the page, under D. "Sector Sarajevo. Commander, General Gobillard and his escort came under cross-fire in the area of Butmir at 2230 hours. The General's vehicle was hit by a single" - I think that probably means bullet - "no casualties, damage to the vehicle. It was not a direct targeting of UNPROFOR." Do you know that UNPROFOR people were caught in a cross-fire on that day, the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I thank the witness. I thank the Chamber. And I, yet again, apologise to the witness for my previous insinuation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony, Mr. Witness. You have provided information the Chamber with a piece of information that was quite new today, namely, the fact that you assembled your reports for the purposes of providing this Tribunal with evidence. And I'm curious to know if you can tell us a bit more about how this came about. Was there an instruction from the Ministry of the Interior, or was it only an instruction from the cantonal Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, to collect evidence and to prepare this evidence for transmission to the criminal tribunal? Can you tell us a little more about what kind of instruction was issued for this purpose, and who issued it and when it was issued and how it was implemented?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: The department for gathering material on genocide, is that what you have in mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question relates to information that you have given us today two or three times, where you told us that you made these reports for the purpose of providing the Tribunal with evidence. So I want you to expand a little more on that and to ask you, according to which instructions did you prepare these reports, and was it an instruction for collecting evidence for the Tribunal, for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Well, it was at the level of the city of Sarajevo that a department was set up for gathering information and documents on the genocide. Any information obtained from victims or people who suffered some sort of trauma during the war was gathered by us. They would come to us and they would give us statements. I wasn't alone. There were several inspectors gathering information. It was information on the aggressor to the west and to the east, because this was going on in some areas that were under the HVO at the time and also in the areas under Serbian control. We compiled all those statements. We drew up reports for both sides, and that's how we submitted those documents for possible use by the Tribunal. If that's what you had in mind, sir. That was the whole department doing that, gathering information on the genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask, was the department set up specifically for the purpose of gathering information for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who set this institution up?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BUCO
utterances.text: [In English] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that constitutes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could be excused as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Docherty, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as its next witness, the Prosecution calls Mr. Huso Palo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name, please, and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Huso Palo; 6th of October, 1932.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Palo --

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Huso Palo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Palo, have you ever worked as a tram driver in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: From the 23rd of March until the end of the war, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you said the 23rd of March, what year was that in, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Palo, on the 24th of February, 1996, did you meet with an investigator from this Tribunal and make a statement?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes. At Nedzarici, on the premises of your Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And since arriving in The Hague to testify, have you taken the opportunity to read that statement over carefully?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: I didn't read anything. She asked me questions. I just answered questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Perhaps my question wasn't clear. You arrived in The Hague three or four days ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes, last Friday, on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And earlier this week, do you remember meeting with me and an interpreter in the offices here in this building?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: At that meeting, did you have an opportunity to re-read the statement that you had given in 1996?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Palo, my question was: Did you read it three days ago?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did read the instructions. The oath, not the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Palo, did you three days ago re-read --

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: -- in the Bosnian language the statement that you gave in 1996?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't. I didn't. Can't say that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Palo, would you like to see a copy of the statement that you gave in 1996?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Well, you might. Yes, yes. Please, my eyesight is not very good, but I'm sure I can handle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Give us just one moment, Mr. Palo, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's been e-mailed to the court officer for printing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so that everyone in the courtroom could see it, the statement has the 65 ter number 2889. And I wonder if I could ask that that be displayed on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Palo, could you just take a look at what is in front of you and let us know if that is something that you have seen earlier this week here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Everything is true, what I have just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, based on the last answer, I'll offer into evidence the 65 ter number 2889, the ICTY witness statement of Mr. Huso Palo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is already an exhibit bearing Exhibit number D36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I think at this time that will conclude my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would ask the court deputy to check on that exhibit again, as my colleague, who keeps records very well, says D36 was a photograph. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I was trying to wrap up my previous examination, and in my haste I forgot to tender this document as an exhibit. It's the UNPROFOR report. Just to avoid returning to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is our document, DD00- -- DD00-0436. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This number, D36, perhaps it would be better to sort this out now because that was presented by the Prosecution and can cannot be a D number; it should be P something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: My memory is that this document was shown to a witness this morning, Ms. Sabanic. I don't remember, though, if it was tendered or if it was simply shown to the witness. And our information is also that D36 is an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in that case, D36 is a photograph; it's not a statement. I would have liked to see it again, but it's not D36.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I shall introduce myself. Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I work for the Paris bar association. If we have time, we shall start the cross-examination this afternoon, but I might not have time to do much. I would like to ask you a few questions concerning your statement, the one you have just read, the one you have before you. And you recognise that this is your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, we had not given a number to the UNPROFOR report tendered by Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the UNPROFOR report will be Exhibit D38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were you able to verify what D36 was? The court deputy is working on that. Well, we just have a few minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, do you remember having made two statements? One was made in Nedzarici and given to the Office of the Prosecutor, as you said, and the other statement was given to the police that conducted the investigation and what happened on the tram which you were driving on the 23rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's have a look at these two statements now. Firstly, let's look at the first statement you gave on the 24th of November, 1994, which you gave to the policemen who were in charge of investigating the accident that occurred on the 23rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this could be displayed on the screen, please. For everybody concerned, this is number 694, page 17. It's a 65 ter document. It's the same document as the one previously shown today. This should be document D35.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what I should say. What I said here is all true. As for everything else, I don't know. I don't remember. I remember giving two statements at Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, it's time for the adjournment. Witness, you'll have to return on Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9.00. Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you're not to discuss your evidence with anybody. We're adjourned to 9.00 a.m. on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
